research_question: What is the effect of resistance training during anticancer therapy, compared with no training, on cancer-related fatigue measured at 12 weeks or less, in people with cancer?
control_label: no training (usual care or waitlist control)
outcome_description: Cancer-related fatigue measured at 12 weeks or less from baseline/intervention start
positive_direction: A positive effect size indicates lower fatigue (better clinical outcome) in the resistance training group compared to the control group.
search_queries: resistance training anticancer therapy cancer related fatigue trial
strength exercise oncology fatigue controlled study
resistance exercise chemotherapy fatigue quantitative outcome
inclusion_criteria: Studies of individuals with cancer receiving active anticancer therapy (e.g., chemotherapy, radiation, hormone therapy)
Interventions incorporating resistance training compared against a no-training or usual care control condition
Quantitative assessment of cancer-related fatigue measured at or before 12 weeks
exclusion_criteria: Not an original empirical study (systematic reviews, meta-analyses, editorials, commentaries, and theoretical papers are excluded)
No comparison between a resistance training group and a non-exercise or usual-care control group
No quantitative outcome data for fatigue that can produce an effect size (e.g., means and standard deviations, change scores, or test statistics)
Fatigue assessed exclusively after 12 weeks or completely unrelated to resistance training during active anticancer therapy
moderators_to_extract: anticancer therapy type (chemotherapy, radiation therapy, androgen deprivation/hormone therapy)
supervision level (fully supervised, partially supervised, or unsupervised)
effect_size_note: Standardized mean difference (Hedges g) calculated such that positive values indicate reduced fatigue in the resistance training group.
